name: Latvian
catalog_quote: Latvian has word-initial stress. In modern, urban dialects, the word initial syllable is the only one that carries extra prominence.
sweep_summary: Three sweep items for Latvian. (1) Kariņš 1996 BLS 22 'Optimal stress feet in Latvian' — fetched sources open (BLS site needs a browser UA; scan scanned at 300 dpi), read: first syllable receives primary stress regardless of weight (undominated ALIGNHEAD), secondary stress via moraic trochees (short words) / syllabic trochees (long words) from Endzelins 1922 data — confirms fixed-strict and offers a secondary-stress rule. (2) Kariņš 1996 UPenn dissertation — not in the UPenn repository (three DSpace API queries, 0 hits), ProQuest/print only; medium priority, expected to restate the same analysis at length. (3) Ekblom 1933 'Die lettischen Akzentarten' — 80-page experimental-phonetic study of the three syllable intonations from Endzelins' own pronunciation (LIBRIS record; described first-hand in Kariņš 1997 p.186); prosody but not word stress; no digital copy found; low priority. Bonus: Kariņš 1997 BLS 23 'Lexical tone and stress in Latvian' (wishlist item previously unfetched) also fetched sources and read: 'Main word stress in Latvian occurs on the first syllable of a word' (p.186), tone independent of stress, and a documented non-initial-stress lexeme nekad 'never' (p.193) — refines (lexical exceptions in ne- compounds). Best new first-hand statement: Kariņš 1996 BLS p.210; it confirms but does not supersede the catalog's deciding source (Endzelin 1923 reference grammar). new_statements.locator: p.210, §3 (introducing undominated constraints (5)); secondary-stress data pp.208-209 examples (1)-(3), all from Endzelins 1922
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial primary stress, weight-insensitive, with trochaic secondary stress: moraic trochees L->R in 2-3 syllable words, syllabic trochees L->R in 4-5 syllable words, plus stem-stressed morphological exceptions. Confirms the catalog's fixed-strict (initial) coding and supplies a secondary-stress rule (srule) the record lacks. The companion 1997 paper (p.186 'Main word stress in Latvian occurs on the first syllable of a word'; p.193 nekad 'never' with primary stress on the second syllable) adds that a small class of ne- compounds has non-initial primary stress — a lexical exception, not a change of type.

sources.locator: p.210, §3 'An OT account of Latvian stress', text introducing constraint (5) ALIGNHEAD; data pp.208-209 (1)-(3); p.208 §1
sources.note: Primary stress is on the first syllable regardless of weight (undominated ALIGNHEAD + trochaic feet). Secondary stress exists (contra Halle & Vergnaud 1987 / Goldsmith 1990; supported by Karins' 1995-96 experimental work): short words (2-3 syll.) build moraic trochees L->R, long words (4-5 syll.) build syllabic trochees L->R, with some ternary and stem-stressed exceptions; all stress data taken from Endzelins 1922. Confirms fixed initial primary stress and adds the secondary-stress pattern (weight-sensitive in short words, alternating in long words).

sources.citation: Hualde, José Ignacio & Tomas Riad. 2014. Word accent and intonation in Baltic. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2014 (Dublin), 669-672. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2014-122
sources.quote: 'In Latvian, stress generally falls on the initial syllable of the word. If the stressed syllable is heavy ... a three-way contrast in accent type in syllables is said to obtain.' Conclusion: 'Latvian having developed fixed initial stress, and Lithuanian retaining mobile stress.'

sources.citation: Daugavet, Anna. 2010. Syllable length in Latvian and Lithuanian: searching for the criteria. Baltic Linguistics 1, 83-114. doi:10.32798/bl.436
sources.quote: 'In Lithuanian, syllable length can influence the position of primary stress, while in Latvian it is one of the factors in secondary stress assignment.' ... 'In Latvian (Fig. 4), final syllables receive secondary stress only if they are long.' (refers to Daugaviete 2005, 2008 for accounts of Latvian secondary stress). Silent on primary-stress placement beyond presupposing it; adds weight-sensitive secondary stress not in our record (srule empty).

sources.quote: Main word stress in Latvian occurs on the first syllable of a word (see Endzelins, 1922). [p.186] ... The figure in (12) illustrates that a rise in pitch occurs over the primarily stressed syllable even if this syllable is non-initial. [p.189] ... (16) Phonological representations of the words vaga 'furrow' (primary stress on the first syllable) and nekad 'never' (primary stress on the second syllable) [p.193]
sources.locator: p.186 §1 Introduction; p.189 (text before fig. 12); p.193 (16)
sources.note: Main word stress on the first syllable (citing Endzelins 1922); lexical tone (level/falling/broken) is independent of stress and occurs on all heavy syllables; primary stress is phonologically a H tone. Notes a lexical exception with non-initial primary stress: nekad 'never' stressed on the second syllable (ne- compounds), with pitch data from a Riga speaker. Confirms initial primary stress; refines by documenting a non-initial-stress lexeme.
